grammar_notes.heading: Nouns
grammar_notes.text: There are very few short words in Pawnee. Most words are more descriptive and are longer constructions of smaller parts. The shorter words are usually names of common objects, such as the things named in this chapter. Words that name things are called nouns, and nouns in Pawnee often end in the suffix -u'. (A suffix is a small part of a word attached to the end of it.) Some nouns in Pawnee are words which have been copied or borrowed from English; when this happens, the word is given a distinct Pawnee pronunciation, and often it is hard to hear the English equivalent. Look at the names for nickel, dime, and quarter above. What English words do they suggest?

grammar_notes.heading: Pronunciation
grammar_notes.text: At first, you may find some sounds of Pawnee hard to pronounce. One of the sounds is the letter r. It is easier to pronounce between vowels. There it sounds like a fast d as in the English word ready, but is softer. Drill: (iri) kiriks (ari) karitki (ira) tirakis When the r begins a word, it is helpful to stick in a very short a just before the r, so that you put the r between vowels. Drill: rakis (arakis) raku' (araku')

grammar_notes.heading: Useful Phrases
grammar_notes.text: 1. Nawa! Hello, okay, now. The old pronunciation of this word is rawa, but the pronunciation and spelling with n is so common, we have included this word as the only one to use n. Common expressions tend to receive unique pronunciations. Notice that the Skidi word for yes (hail) ends with a strong nasal quality (sound coming through the nose). 2. Istu. Again. 3. Suks-paku'. Say it. 4. Aka! Oh my! Gee! 5. Ka? What?

grammar_notes.heading: Indicators
grammar_notes.text: Indicators are Pawnee words which indicate statements, questions, denials, and so on. Ka ru'? Ka ru kisu'? Ti'. Ti kisu'. Kaki'. Kaki kisu'. Is it? Is it a bone? It is. This is. This is a bone. It is not. No. It is not a bone. KIRIKJ RA•TARAWIS?

grammar_notes.heading: A Sound Change
grammar_notes.text: Many Pawnee roots begin with r. This beginning r will change to a t if the last letter of the root before it in a phrase ends with any of the following hard consonants: p, t, k, ts, or s. Note the following example: rakis + rahkata = rakis•tahkata a yellow stick

grammar_notes.heading: Pronunciation
grammar_notes.text: To speak Pawnee well, you must learn to draw out or lengthen certain vowels. It is not possible to make a simple rule that will tell you when to do this. So listen carefully to speakers of Pawnee and to the tapes which accompany these lessons. Listen for the vowels which are drawn out and those which are not. In this way you will learn to pronounce the words in a genuine Pawnee fashion. Here are some examples of simple words with both long and normal (short) vowels in the first syllable of the word: Short Vowels rakis kiriks nawa riwit (rd-kis) (ki-riks) (rd-wa) (ri-wit) wood bead now skunk Long Vowels Pari' (pd-ri ') Pawnee hitu ' (hi-tu ') feather raku' (ra-ku') box kitsu ' (ki-tsu ') liquid In addition, the Skidi pronunciation of a word may keep a syllable short where South Band pronunciation lengthens it. Suks•paku' (SB) (suks pa-ku') You (1) say it! (SK)(suks pd-ku ') You (1) say it! As a serious student of the Pawnee language, you should listen for and imitate these long syllables, and try to get the right quality of the vowel. To help in remembering a long syllable, use a pencil to underline the vowel of the long syllable right in your book. raku ' or raku ' box

grammar_notes.heading: Note On Research
grammar_notes.text: When you write down words you hear from Pawnee speakers, be sure to underline the long syllables.

grammar_notes.heading: Interpretation
grammar_notes.text: Perhaps the most interesting and enjoyable part of studying Pawnee is learning how to interpret Pawnee words, or how to understand the meaning of a word by figuring out its smaller parts or roots. Notice how the two words for snake can be interpreted by comparing them to other words in the lesson. rutki (SB) snake rut + ki = serpent + small thing = snake rakis stick, piece of wood rak + kis = wood + small thing = stick Most Pawnee words are derived or made up from small roots. One of these small roots used to make up words is + kits + or + ki +, which means liquid. kitsu '	liquid kits + u' hetu ' breast het•kitsu ' milk rasitu' ice kira•rasitu' water ki + ra + rasitu ' liquid from ice In addition, most objects in nature, which Engish may name simply river or tree, will be named in Pawnee by a descriptive phrase: ra .ha•pi tree or "it's wood standing" ti r I ha•pi There is a tree. + u + in a line + hat + goes by ti kits•u"hat stream, river or "it's liquid going by"

grammar_notes.heading: Combining Roots
grammar_notes.text: When roots are combined to form phrases, they change spelling. If you know the rules of these spelling changes, you will be able to interpret many words where the roots are disguised by different spellings. Here are some spelling rules which are active in the words given in this chapter. 1. r changes to t after a hard consonant ti rihu it's big ti ha"k•tihu it's big wood 2. w changes to p after a hard consonant ti .wari' he goes about tat•pari '	I go about 3. k drops off before p ti hak•tsa log tira ha•pi tree 4. r changes to h before any consonant hiru ' meadow ti hih•wa yard hir + wa 5. i + lay combine to make e ahitu' fat t'ehit he's fat ti + ahit Notice how these rules can interact: 1. ti + hak + wa + wi it's wood widely vertical _2. ti + hak + pa + wi w becomes p 3. ti + ha_ + pa + wi k drops off 4. ti ha•pa•wi there are trees

grammar_notes.heading: Pronunciation
grammar_notes.text: Remember that all the parts of a phrase are pronounced together without a pause. The last sound of one word will slur over into the beginning of the next word. ti hih•wa grass (ti-hi-hwa) or (ti-hi-wha)

grammar_notes.heading: Verb Phrase
grammar_notes.text: Words which refer to actions or events are called verbs. In English, have is a verb; in Pawnee, t ih-ra is a verb phrase, a group of roots meaning I have it. The first part, tab ., is an introducer, the second, •ra, the verb root meaning have. Introducers In Pawnee, an introducer carries information such as 1) MODE (indicators or markers) how does this information relate to what the speakers know? 2) PERSON: (markers) who is involved? 3) NUMBER: (markers) how many are involved? introducer•verb = mode + person + verb root tah•ra ta + h + ra I'm telling you + I + have I have it. ta +s +ra I'm telling you + you + have You have it. ra + s + ra we know + you + have (that) you have it. introducerverb = mode + person + number + verb root ta'hrarra ta + h + rar + ra I tell you + I + them + have I have some (them). 'INTRODUCER = MODE + PERSON + NUMBER Mode can be indicated either by a marker or an indicator which is joined to the introducer. The indicator may change its last letter according to who is the subject. Ta'h•ra. I have it. Kakah•ra. I don't have it. VERB SET: Tah .ra I have it. (May be used to play a classroom game like "Who's got the button?") Question: Take ra•ra? Who has it? Responses: Tah•ra. I have it. Tas•ta. You have it. TI ra. He or she has it. tas-ta ras•ta Question: Take rararra? Responses: Tahrarra. Tastarra. Tirarra. Si tahrarra. Si tastarra. Si tirarra. Tahraktarra Tastaktarra Tihrarra Who has them? I have them. You have them. He or she has them. We (2) have them. You (2) have them. They (2) have them. We (3+) have them. You (3+) have them. They (3+) have them.

grammar_notes.heading: Plurals
grammar_notes.text: In English, a noun which refers to more than one thing is called a plural noun, and it ends in -s, the plural suffix. (Examples: dogs, cats, trees.) In Pawnee, there is really no plural ending, and any noun can refer to one thing, two things, or three or more things. pita a man, some men rakis a stick, some sticks hitu '	a feather, some feathers Plurality is usually indicated by markers in the introducer of the verb phrase. Tah•ra. I have it. Thhrarra. I have some. + rar + plural (more than one) Tahra'ktarra. We have them. + rak + more than one of us Usually, the plural subject is marked by + rak +, the plural object by + rar +. There are other plural markers such as + it + for they and + atsir + for two of us, but these plurals are used in only a few places. Tihrarra. They (3+) have them. ti + it + rarra Tatsih•wari'. We (you and I) are going about. to + atsir + wari'

grammar_notes.heading: Notes
grammar_notes.text: Position of Objects When talking about any object in Pawnee, you must consider its position or attitude: your head "sits, " (+ ku) almost every other part of your body "hangs" (+ ta). Spelling Rule When i follows u, it drops out. So ti + ku + iks = tiku 'ks, and the remainder of the root joins the introducer, in this case.

grammar_notes.heading: More On The Verb Phrase
grammar_notes.text: A verb phrase is any group of written words which includes an introducer. To avoid confusion, we will talk of introducers being composed of markers; every other meaningful part of a verb phrase will be a root or will be composed of roots.

grammar_notes.heading: Passive Introducers
grammar_notes.text: To say "it hurts" Pawnee uses a form of the introducer which means "it does it to me." ti + I'm telling you that it .. . + ku . . . to me (person marker, first person object) tiku + perks + taari' it does it to me + head + hurts Tiku•paks•taari'. My head hurts.

grammar_notes.heading: Physical Possession
grammar_notes.text: To express physical possession of body parts, the marker ri + is used in the introducer, following the modal marker (indicator) ti, and followed by the person marker. mode + phys. poss. + person + noun + verb ti + ri + t + kirik + to Ti rit•kirik•ta. Here is my eye.

grammar_notes.heading: Completed And Incomplete Action
grammar_notes.text: The simplest form of a verb is the perfect form. In this form the verb indicates action or events already completed. Tiku'ks•taa. My hand has been hurt. (my hand got hurt) Perfect Tiku'ks•taari'. My hand is hurting. (my hand hurts) Imperfect The imperfect form indicates action or events still happening, incomplete action. This is the form used in this chapter, though the perfect form could easily be substituted in the dialogues.

grammar_notes.heading: Commands
grammar_notes.text: In Pawnee, commands to the hearer use the perfect form of the verb, and build an introducer out of the second person (hearer) marker s +, the command marker +uks, and number markers si + (two hearers) and +rak (three or more hearers). Tas•pa"ku'. You have said it. Suks•paku'. You (1) say it! s + uks + wak + u' you + do it + say it + completed Sisuks•paku'. You (2) say it! Suksta•pdku ' . You (3+) say it. s + uks + rak + waki + u' VERB SETS: Commands and Responses (Imperative and Perfect Forms) Single Person Suks•paku'. Tat•paku'. You (1) say it. I have said it. Suks•pitit. Tat•pitit. You (1) sit down. I have sat down. Stiks•at. You (1) go (away). Two Persons (Dual) Sisukspaku'. You (2) say it. Sisukspitit. You (2) sit down. Sisuks .pa. You (2) go (away). Suksta-paku'. *s + uks + rak + wak + u' You (3+) say it. Suksta•pitit. You (3+) sit down. Stiksta•pu'. You (3+) go (away). Tat•at. I have gone (away). Sitat•paku'. We (2) have said it. Sitat .pitit. We (2) have sat down. Sitat•pa. We (2) have gone (away). Tahrapaku'. to + t + rak + wak + u' We (3+) have said it. Tahra .pitit. We (3+) have sat down. Tahra•pu'. We (3+) have gone (away).

grammar_notes.heading: Irregular Roots
grammar_notes.text: Normally, the root form of any particular verb, say eat, will stay the same, no matter who is eating or when they ate. However, some common verbs in Pawnee will have different forms for different subjects. Notice the roots for go are +at for one person, +wa (+pa) for two persons, and +wu (+pu) for three or more persons as subjects. This is somewhat like English I go and I went, rather than I goed. *SPELLING RULE Remember, w goes to p after a hard consonant, and k drops out before p.

grammar_notes.heading: Pre Verbs
grammar_notes.text: Some verbs in Pawnee are accompanied by markers which indicate certain relationships like those indicated by English prepositions in to it, for it, and on it. Two of these markers are + ut and + ur and are included in the introducer, which is why they are called preverbs. ti•ari' he's becoming tut•ari ' he 's making it or doing it (tu-td-ri') ti + ut + ari it is + for him + becoming

grammar_notes.heading: Person Markers
grammar_notes.text: In Pawnee verb phrases, the introducer will tell who is being talked about, that is, who the subject and object of the sentence are. When a single letter or root is used, we call this a person marker. There are four main person markers in Pawnee: 1. Subjects (who is doing it) + t first person, I or we (speaker or any group which includes him) tat. kikat I am crying sitat•kikat we (2) are crying + s second person, you tas•kikat you are crying sitas .kikat you (2) are crying 2. Objects (who is experiencing it) + ku first person, to me, to us tiku'tskipi I am sleepy sitiku'tskipi we (2) are sleepy tikurak•itskipi we (3+) are sleepy + a second person to you ta 'tskipi you (1) are sleepy sita'tskipi you (2) are sleepy tarak•itskipi you (3+) are sleepy 3. Third Person: he, she, it Third person refers to someone or something who is neither the speaker nor the hearer. In English, the words he, she, and it refer also to sex and the difference between a person and a thing. Pawnee makes no such distinctions. Ti pahaat means he is red or she is red or it is red. grammar_notes.text: There are verb phrases in Pawnee which describe nouns by further specifying which object or person is being referred to, and often describing its position. grammar_notes.heading: Pawnee Kinship
grammar_notes.text: One of the cultural habits of the old-time Pawnees that still survives today is the unique non-English way of using kinship terms. There seem to be complicated rules for figuring out what to call someone, but since the English system has been mixed in, the important thing to consider is the difference between a "respect" and a "joking" relationship, as suggested by Weltfish (1965: Chapter 3). A boy or man calls a woman atira and she calls him tiki or son if she is responsible for his welfare and for giving him advice on how to act properly. This represents a relationship of respect, and a man who calls a woman atira will call her sisters and daughters atira also, as relationships of respect are inherited. Atias is another term of respect. In the old days, the tribal agent was called atias or father and other white persons were likely to be called irari or brother, friend. Terms of a joking relationship are atipat or apat or grampa and atika or gramma. A man may call a woman atika to represent a more informal relationship and a woman may call a man apat or grampa to represent an informal, familiar relationship which calls for teasing and joking. Joking relationships are more easily created and two persons may easily choose to call each other, for example, apat or grampa and taka or sonny, whereas the use of atias, atira, and other terms of respect are more strict and inherited. KI Rid RA. KU?

grammar_notes.heading: Past Tense
grammar_notes.text: There is one marker in Pawnee which refers to time. This is the marker +uks, which follows the person marker in the introducer and means in a time past. We have seen that +uks also marks the command form, but in that usage, the introducer has no marker of mode. Suks .atku. Tasuks•atku. Listen! You listened. The u in +uks is a strong vowel which causes the a in modal marker +ra and i in modal marker ti + to drop out. question mode person past verb kiru +ra +0 +uks +ku kiru +ra +uks +ku (a drops out) Niru ruks•ku? Where was it? Pawnee does not use a letter or root to refer to the third person. It's the fact that no person marker is present which means third person. The symbol is used to denote the absence of a marker in the interpretation. tat .kiikat tat. =ta + t tas .kikat tas. = to + s ti .kikat ti. = ti + I am crying first person you are crying second person he, she, it is crying third person Notice also that the modal marker has a different vowel for third person. mode person past root root ti +1 +uks +ka +ku' ti +uks +ka +ku' Tuks .kaku '. He was in the house.

grammar_notes.heading: Nouns In A Verb Phrase
grammar_notes.text: In Pawnee, a noun can often be included inside the verb phrase, as we saw in Lesson 3. That was a case of subject nouns being included. Nouns of location can also be included. First they are reduced to a root form and then inserted before the verb. 3g hatur•raru' road ti•kaarit he is standing in it ti +hatur +ka +arit r becomes h before k +ka + "in" ti +hatuh +ka +arit ti•hattih•kaarit he's standing in the road

grammar_notes.heading: Object Verb Phrase
grammar_notes.text: If there is only one noun in the sentence, it can come either before or after the verb, according to what is the most important new information in the sentence. Rikutski ti pahaat. The bird is red. Ti pahaat rikutski. The bird is red. Normally, what is important or in focus is first in the sentence; what is understood or presumed is last. When two nouns appear in the same sentence, the subject comes directly before the verb phrase, the object comes last, and time words may follow the object. Pita ti•kuwutit rahurahki pitsikat. subject verb phr. object time word The man killed a deer , in the winter.

Time and Subject Indicators: hiri and we Most statements in Pawnee begin with a time or subject indicator. We is used to begin almost any statement; it is a syllable which comes just before the introducer and means now or then. Really, it means at that certain time and is used to point out a time which may not be already understood by the hearer. Hiri means that thing or that place and refers to the real subject of a sentence which is known by the hearer but not necessarily understood without this word to point it out. If you are using one of the verb phrases given in this book to make a statement to somebody, you should normally start with we. Ta.tuks•at. I went We tatuks•at. I went (then) (or, I had gone) VERB SET (Various aspects): to drink Tat .kika'. I have drunk, I drank. (perfect aspect) Tat•kikahu ' . I am drinking. (imperfect aspect) Tatuks•kika'. I drank, I had drunk. (past tense, perfect aspect) Tatuks•kikahu'. I was drinking. (past tense, imperfect aspect) Suks•kika ' . Drink! (Command) The Suggestive Mode Some commands are given like suggestions, such as the comparison of "Shut the door" and "Would you shut the door?". These commands take the form of normal verb phrases with a suggestive modal indicator ke+. Tiku•'u. He gave it to me. Kesku•'u. Tasku•'u. Give it to me. You should give it to me. You gave it to me. grammar_notes.heading: Adjectives
grammar_notes.text: ru ti ra•pdrihrit ru tuks•ta•pdrihrit ti kasis ti katus ta rara•rdsitu' ta ta rd ritu' td taris kakd taris it is smooth it was smooth it's hard it's flat it's cold = indicator "this" it's hot it's heavy it's light (not heavy) Antonyms In English many adjectives come in pairs: big/small, light/ heavy. These opposites are called antonym s. In Pawnee, almost any adjective can be made into its antonym by using the negative indicator kaki or kaka. More on Indicators We have already pointed out that the model indicator ti is used for third person subjects, ta for first and second person. In the same way, the negative model indicator kaki is used for third person subjects, kaka for first and second persons. tat•at I went (have gone) tas•at you went tf•'at he went kakat•at I didn't go kakas•at you didn't go kakI 'at he didn't go In addition, there are adjective and verb roots which take the indicator ta, even though the subject may be third person. ta•rutsa' he (has) lifted it ta rara•rasitu it's cold ta na ritu' it's hot to taxis it's heavy Notice that these verb phrases imply an effect on the subject, like heat or weight.

(SB) Don't touch! SUBJECT AND OBJECT: Transitive Verbs The noun that refers to the doer is the subject. The noun that refers to the done-to thing is the object. Verbs that describe actions like seeing and killing may appear with both subject and object: these are called transitive verbs. The subject always appears before the object, if both are named by a noun; the English order subject-verb-object is acceptable, but old Pawnee speakers preferred both nouns together . Pita ti•kuwutit kuruks. The man has killed a bear. Pita kuruks ti .kuwutit. The man has killed a bear. TRANSITIVE VERB SET: Tut•erit. He has seen it (he saw it). Question: Take rut•erit? Tatut .erit. grammar_notes.heading: Verb-Final K
grammar_notes.text: No Pawnee word ends in k. If there is a k in the underlying root form of a verb, it will show up only before a verb suffix (ending) such as the habitual +usuku ' or the imperfect +us or +u'. grammar_notes.heading: Future Tense
grammar_notes.text: What is called in English future tense is expressed in Pawnee by the suffix +ta. It comes as the last part of a verb phrase, and means in a time yet to come. The future marker can occur as (h)ista or 'sta, the perfect (completed) aspect, or as usta, imperfect aspect. Tatutari'sta. I'll do it. (future completed) Tatut•ari .usta. I'll be doing it. (future incomplete) Tatut•a•wahri•usta. I'll be working. Months of the Year Any one of these words can be used in place of rahesa ' in the dialogues. grammar_notes.heading: Primary And Secondary Verb Phrases
grammar_notes.text: Each of the verb phrases we have studied so far has been a primary verb phrase, which means it can be spoken by itself as a complete sentence. When two verb phrases are used together as in tatitska ratkti u•ta I want to go, there is a primary and also a secondary phrase. In English, we often use the word to to mark these verbs. In Pawnee, the introducer of a secondary phrase includes the markers ra + and +ku, with the person marker coming in between. In this chapter, we deal only with the future form of secondary verbs, the form that would naturally go with the primary verb: I want to (do something in the future). There are other forms and meanings of secondary verbs. raku•wa .waktit to speak (a language) (secondary, perfect) we raku•sakur•isat•ta when the sun goes down (see Lesson 17) raku•ka .pihat dwelling (see Reading)

grammar_notes.text: Here are two conversations which should be memorized and practiced by anyone who wants to be able to identify himself as a Pawnee speaker or encourage elders to speak Pawnee. grammar_notes.heading: Cultural Note
grammar_notes.text: It is traditional Pawnee courtesy to serve coffee or other refreshments without asking the guest whether or not he or she would like some. If the guest shows up at dinner time, he is immediately shown to a place at the table. No opportunity is given for polite refusal, as is the European custom, and visitors are expected to visit before doing business.

grammar_notes.heading: Epilogue
grammar_notes.text: Our Way (Our People) LIVING PAWNEE: Speaking, Singing, Writing. The Pawnee language lives when people talk to each other in their own way. Speech and conversation are the main ways but not the only ways people talk to each other. Singing and writing are important ways in which people talk with or communicate to other people. Listening to songs and reading any written material can help you learn Pawnee. The special Pawnee language material in this chapter can be used for classroom or private enjoyment of this written, sung and recited material.

grammar_notes.heading: Where We Used To Live
grammar_notes.text: This our Pawnee tribe is made up of four bands; we are these: Tsawii, Kitkahahki, Pitahawirata and Tskiri. And it (the tribe) used to live, it is said, in mud lodges near the Platte ("Flat") River. Twice a year they went hunting. It is said that they killed buffalo and deer, (game). In addition, they planted various things, corn, beans and squash. They would roast corn, and used to make jerky and they dried the beans and squash. Perhaps there were about thirty people dwelling in one mud lodge. Also they would put their horses inside in the winter. It is said that it (the tribe) had (many) customs which were very wonderful. The old ones were apparently sincere (about these things). It must have been good land there where we lived. Those other enemy tribes about (us), attacked us all the time. The leaders, perhaps, decided to come down here to the south. a B u
